title: LLM Gateway Trust Boundaries
html:
LLM Gateway Trust Boundaries

An LLM gateway handles model routing and often holds provider credentials, so its ordinary API callers must not inherit configuration or provider-level authority. The LiteLLM gateway assessment on version 1.77.7 illustrates two separate boundaries: UI-session authorization for administrative configuration and caller-supplied routing configuration for inference. The reported issues were fixed in version 1.83.9.[1]

UI route classification is not authorization

In the assessed LiteLLM version, UI login keys belonged to the litellm-dashboard team. Authorization classified a key as a UI token from that team identifier, regardless of the user's role. The UI route check then accepted any route beginning with an allowlisted prefix. As a result, the /config entry also matched the administrative /config/update handler. That handler required generic authentication but did not independently require PROXY_ADMIN, so a lower-privileged UI session crossed into configuration write access.[1]

This differs from a proxy/backend path-normalization mismatch: the authorization code and handler disagree about the authority of the same route.[1] When reviewing a gateway, compare token classification, exact route and method matching, and the handler's own role check.[1] See web API authorization, 401/403 bypasses, and proxy prefix exemptions for related but distinct boundaries.

Configuration writes reach more than the configuration store

The same LiteLLM configuration update accepted environment-variable values and applied them to the running process. One consumer treated UI_LOGO_PATH as a local path for a FileResponse, without validating that it identified a logo; another read UI_USERNAME and UI_PASSWORD during non-SSO login and assigned PROXY_ADMIN when they matched. Thus a configuration-write permission could become both local-file disclosure and an administrative identity change, depending on the downstream consumer. The response media type does not establish that a served file is an image.[1]

The pass-through endpoint configuration was another downstream sink. Initialization accepted remote S3/GCS adapter targets, downloaded Python modules, and imported them using importlib's exec_module. Import executes top-level code before an adapter instance is used; merely restricting invocation of the adapter would not remove that execution boundary. Treat this as configuration-controlled code loading, not model-file deserialization.[1] For the separate file-read primitive, see file inclusion and path traversal.

Per-request model routing can leak gateway credentials

LiteLLM's client-side credential feature accepted a user_config object in an LLM request. The assessed route created a temporary litellm.Router from that object, including its model list and provider api_base. A caller-controlled provider destination could receive the gateway's outbound completion request and configured provider authentication headers. Restrictions on top-level api_base or api_key fields did not cover this separate nested configuration path. This is a credential-bearing SSRF boundary, rather than a prompt-injection issue.[1]

For an authorized gateway assessment, compare every path that can construct a router or provider client, including per-request configuration, against the destination and credential policy used by the normal configured route.[1] The SSRF guide covers general server-side destination control; the gateway-specific failure is allowing a less-trusted request object to select a destination while reusing privileged outbound credentials.[1]

Guardrail registration can bypass a UI-only sandbox

A gateway's code-test path and code-registration path may have different validation. In LiteLLM before v1.82.0, the UI custom-guardrail test rejected dangerous syntax and executed with __builtins__ = {}, but POST /guardrails compiled the submitted custom_code with exec(compile(...), exec_globals) without either check. Python inserts builtins into a globals dictionary that lacks __builtins__, so module-level imports and commands ran when the guardrail was registered, before any inference call. The later apply_guardrail callback could expose a stored result through its block reason.[2][3]

For an authorized test, compare the test and registration handlers rather than assuming a successful UI sandbox test proves registration safe. The reported pre-fix request shape was:[2]

POST /guardrails HTTP/1.1
Authorization: Bearer <master_key>
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "guardrail": {
    "guardrail_name": "probe",
    "litellm_params": {
      "guardrail": "custom_code", "mode": "pre_call", "default_on": true,
      "custom_code": "import os\nresult = os.popen('id').read()\ndef apply_guardrail(inputs, request_data, input_type):\n    return {'action': 'block', 'reason': result}"
    }
  }
}

The registration endpoint also accepted ordinary API keys because it lacked a PROXY_ADMIN check. Where no master key or JWT/OAuth2 authentication was configured, the pre-fix auth handler assigned PROXY_ADMIN even to anonymous requests. The fix changed the no-auth role to INTERNAL_USER, added guardrail admin checks, and validated and restricted builtins during registration. These role and code-execution boundaries are separate from the MCP token-fallback issue.[2][3]

Admin pass-through routes can proxy cloud metadata

LiteLLM's pass-through endpoint feature lets an administrator configure an HTTP target and optionally append subpaths. Unlike the per-request user_config routing issue above, this requires configuration-write authority; the feature itself is intended to trust administrators. In the reported deployment, the target was not checked against private or link-local addresses.[2][4] Before v1.83.0, ordinary authenticated keys could also reach /config/update because it lacked an administrator role check; see UI route classification for the related configuration-write boundary.[2][6]

With that authority and network reachability from the proxy to EC2 metadata, a route such as the following exposes metadata through the gateway. The include_subpath flag makes /meta/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ map under /latest/.[2][4]

POST /config/pass_through_endpoint HTTP/1.1
Authorization: Bearer <master_key>
Content-Type: application/json

{"path":"/meta","target":"http://169.254.169.254/latest/","headers":{},"include_subpath":true}

The Cloud SSRF guide covers the IMDSv2 token exchange; this route must permit its PUT request and relay both metadata headers.[5] LiteLLM's generic pass-through header handling strips the x-pass- prefix before forwarding, so x-pass-X-aws-ec2-metadata-token-ttl-seconds: 21600 and x-pass-X-aws-ec2-metadata-token: <token> can supply those headers.[2][7] The proxy must reach IMDS, the token response must traverse the configured hop limit, and the token request must not carry X-Forwarded-For.[5] The gateway-specific variation is the admin-controlled persistent route plus request-header relay.

References

  • [2] Wiz — Off Guard: Breaking LiteLLM from Authentication Bypass to Cloud Compromise
  • [3] LiteLLM PR #22095 — fix unauthenticated RCE and sandbox escape in custom code guardrail
  • [4] LiteLLM — Create Pass Through Endpoints
  • [5] AWS — How Instance Metadata Service Version 2 works
  • [6] LiteLLM advisory — unrestricted proxy configuration endpoint
  • [7] LiteLLM pass-through header forwarding implementation
